name: Bitcoin
executive_summary: Bitcoin launched in 2009 as peer-to-peer electronic cash, and seventeen years later at the time of this scoring, that track record shows up in a TradFi score of 80: a fixed 21 million coin supply, deep access through ETFs and regulated custody, and a history with zero protocol-level exploits. The AI score lands much lower at 54, because Bitcoin confirms transactions probabilistically rather than with an instant, guaranteed final settlement, and that's precisely the kind of certainty an autonomous agent needs before it can safely act on a payment. The 26-point gap between the two scores comes down to that one architectural choice: built for slow, battle-tested trust rather than machine-speed certainty.

key_findings: TradFi Approved is Bitcoin's strongest category at 97. Regulated ETFs, professional custody services, and licensed trading venues all exist at scale, giving institutions about as much clean, direct access to Bitcoin as any asset in traditional finance.

Tokenomics & Supply scores 97, near the top of the scale. Bitcoin's 21 million coin cap is fixed and its issuance schedule, which cuts new supply in half on a predictable timer, is transparent and unchangeable. The score moved up from 95 because a large amount of Bitcoin mined in the network's earliest days, believed to belong to its pseudonymous creator, has been inactive for over fifteen years and is treated as dead capital rather than a live supply overhang -- those coins remain technically spendable, which is why the score stops short of a perfect 100.

Privacy & Confidentiality is a clear weak point at 36. Every Bitcoin transaction is permanently visible on a fully public ledger, with no built-in way to hide amounts or participants. Third-party mixing tools that once let users blend their coins with others' for extra privacy have thinned out significantly since several of the services that ran them shut down. Simply not disclosing which address belongs to you offers some privacy, but it's a personal habit, not a network protection, and specialized chain-analysis firms have repeatedly de-anonymized addresses in practice.

Decentralization moved from 52 to 40. Roughly 37% of global Bitcoin mining hashrate is concentrated in the United States by jurisdiction -- a real concentration risk, though it's tempered by how slow and costly it would be for that hashrate to actually relocate: the 2021 China mining ban showed that kind of physical move takes months, not the near-instant switch a miner has between mining pools. That slower-moving risk is why this revision is a calibrated discount rather than a straight mechanical read of the jurisdiction concentration alone.

Bitcoin's TradFi score of 80 sits at the boundary of our top tier. A subsequent revision to the Tokenomics & Supply score widened the cushion underneath that published score somewhat, though a shift of a few points in any single category, in either direction, could still be enough to move Bitcoin into or out of that top band at a future review.

binding_cap.short_note: Capped by Deterministic Finality FAIL -- probabilistic-only PoW settlement, no deterministic finality mechanism.

key_findings: Bitcoin's AI score sits 26 points below its TradFi score, the widest gap between the two frameworks for this chain. The reason is structural: institutions trust Bitcoin deeply, but that trust was built on nearly two decades of slow, battle-tested settlement, not on the fast, mathematically guaranteed finality an autonomous agent needs before it can safely treat a payment as done.

Bitcoin fails our check for fast, guaranteed transaction finality outright, because it only ever confirms transactions probabilistically -- there's no point at which the network formally guarantees a transaction can never be reversed, only that reversal becomes increasingly unlikely over time. That failure caps Bitcoin's AI score at 54, just one point below the next tier up.

Security Posture is Bitcoin's strongest category on the AI framework at 88. Over more than 15 years of continuous operation, the core protocol has never suffered a successful exploit -- the longest clean track record of any chain we score.

watch_items: Two proposed upgrades (known as CTV and OP_CAT) that would expand what Bitcoin's scripting language can do are open for network signaling but haven't been activated yet. If adopted, they'd raise the ceiling on how programmable Bitcoin can be scored.

Two proposals addressing Bitcoin's quantum-computer vulnerability -- a new quantum-resistant address format, and a plan to eventually retire older, more vulnerable address types -- are formally documented as of February 2026 but remain in draft and testnet only, with no live mainnet activation yet. Separately, expert estimates of when a quantum computer capable of breaking Bitcoin's current signature scheme might exist have shifted earlier during 2026 research, though there's still no single agreed-upon timeline.

There's no credible near-term path for Bitcoin to pass our fast-finality check. This isn't a maturity issue that more development time would fix -- it's a fundamental result of how Bitcoin's proof-of-work settlement is designed.

Bitcoin's Decentralization score (40) reflects an infrastructure/geographic concentration check layered on top of the existing mining-pool concentration measure -- see above. The Tokenomics & Supply score (97) reflects the adopted treatment of long-dormant, pre-2010 coins as dead capital rather than a live supply overhang.
